summary: Explains why the Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP) was developed: to give retransmission-based reliability over links with very long round-trip times or frequent interruptions. Interplanetary communication is the main example. It is the first of a series of related documents, and it is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Deep-space communication can take minutes and may stop when a spacecraft is out of view. RFC 5325 explains why LTP was designed to transfer data reliably without waiting for short, continuous connections.

questions: why was licklider transmission protocol developed
subtitle: Why deep-space links need reliable transfer that can tolerate long delays and interruptions

tldr.problem: Deep-space links have very long round-trip delays, interruptions, and limited contact times that make ordinary TCP behavior unsuitable.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5325 explains LTP's one-way sessions, reliable red data, best-effort green data, selective reports, deferred sending, and timers informed by link state.
tldr.outcome: This Experimental RFC gives the motivation and overview for LTP. It is not an Internet Standard and is not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 5325 is an Experimental RFC published in September 2008. Its IESG note says it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard; the supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Deep-Space Link Environment
sections.content:
Interplanetary links have propagation delays measured in minutes. The RFC gives an Earth-to-Europa round-trip time of 66 to 100 minutes and explains that a planet can block line of sight, interrupting communication.

Contact with the Deep Space Network is scheduled, and a transmission may wait hours, days, or weeks for a contact period. A protocol must therefore handle queued data and long periods without a return message.
sections.plainLanguage: A deep-space message can take a long time to receive a reply, and the link may be unavailable for a while. Sending systems must keep data until a contact period resumes.

sections.title: Why TCP and SCTP Are a Poor Fit
sections.content:
The RFC explains that TCP throughput can become very low when round-trip times are long and losses occur. TCP also uses a connection handshake and slow start, which can consume a large part of a short contact window.

SCTP can carry multiple data streams over an association, but it still requires round trips to establish the association before application data flows. Deep-space data flows are often mainly one-way, with different rates in the two directions.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols that wait for several replies before sending data waste time on a link where each reply takes a long time. Deep-space traffic may also be much heavier in one direction.

sections.title: LTP Sessions and Data Types
sections.content:
LTP sessions are unidirectional and do not negotiate setup with a handshake. Each block can contain a red part, which the receiver acknowledges and the sender retransmits if needed, and a green part, which is delivered when received but is not retransmitted.

The sender marks checkpoints that prompt reception reports. Those reports identify the ranges of red data received, so the sender can retransmit missing ranges rather than the whole block.
sections.plainLanguage: LTP can mark some data as requiring confirmation and other data as best effort. Reports identify missing reliable data so the sender can resend only what is needed.

sections.title: Deferred Sending and Retransmission
sections.content:
LTP may generate a segment when the link cannot send it. It queues the segment until a link-state cue indicates that transmission is possible. Reports and acknowledgments use an internal operations queue ahead of application data.

The timer for a report or acknowledgment uses the known one-way light time, doubled for a round trip, plus a margin for processing and queuing. LTP suspends timers when link-state cues say the remote engine cannot respond, then resumes them when communication is available.
sections.plainLanguage: LTP stores segments until the link is available. It estimates when replies should arrive using light time and pauses its timers during known interruptions.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The RFC says radio links may let unintended receivers listen to or manipulate LTP segments. Because LTP keeps state for long periods and uses long timeouts, denial-of-service attacks can be especially disruptive.

The RFC describes optional LTP authentication and cookie extensions in a separate extension document. It identifies RFC 5325 as Experimental and says it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Forged segments can consume LTP resources or interfere with a transfer. This RFC is an Experimental motivation document, and it points to a separate document for security extensions.
